      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">HIV</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Human Immunodeficiency Virus</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p><span class="qt0">HIV</span> stands for <span class="qt0">human immunodeficiency virus. HIV</span> harms your immune system by destroying a type of white blood cell that helps your body fight infection. This puts you at risk for other infections and diseases.</p>What is AIDS?<p>AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. It is the final stage of infection with <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. It happens when the body's immune system is badly damaged because of the virus. Not everyone with <span class="qt0">HIV</span> develops AIDS.</p>How does <span class="qt0">HIV</span> spread?<p><span class="qt0">HIV</span> is spread through certain body fluids from a person who has <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. This can happen:</p><ul><li>By having unprotected vaginal or anal sex with a person who has <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. "Unprotected" means not using condoms or medicine to treat or prevent <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. This is the most common way that it spreads.</li><li>By sharing drug needles.</li><li>Through contact with the blood of a person with <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li><li>From mother to fetus during pregnancy.</li><li>From mother to baby during, childbirth, or breastfeeding.</li></ul>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, but certain groups have a higher risk of getting it:</p><ul><li>People who have another sexually transmitted infection (STI). Having an STI can increase your risk of getting or spreading <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li><li>People who inject drugs with shared needles.</li><li>Gay and bisexual men.</li><li>Black/African Americans and Hispanic/Latino Americans. They make up a higher proportion of new <span class="qt0">HIV</span> diagnoses and people with <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, compared to other races and ethnicities.</li><li>People who engage in risky sexual behaviors, such as not using condoms or medicine to prevent or treat <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li></ul><p>Factors such as stigma, discrimination, income, education, and geographic region can also affect people's risk for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p>The first signs of <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection may be flu-like symptoms:</p><ul><li>Fever</li><li>Chills</li><li>Rash</li><li>Night sweats (heavy sweating during sleep)</li><li>Muscle aches</li><li>Sore throat</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Swollen lymph nodes</li><li>Mouth ulcers</li></ul><p>These symptoms may come and go within two to four weeks. This stage is called acute <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection.</p><p>If the infection is not treated, it becomes chronic <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection. Often, there are no symptoms during this stage. If it is not treated, eventually the virus will weaken your body's immune system. Then the infection will progress to AIDS. This is the late stage of <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection. Because your immune system is badly damaged, your body cannot fight off other infections, called opportunistic infections (OIs). OIs are infections that happen more frequently or are more severe in people who have weakened immune systems.</p><p>Some people may not feel sick during the earlier stages of <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection. So the only way to know for sure whether you have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> is to get tested.</p>How do I know if I have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p>A blood test can tell if you have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection. Your health care provider can do the test, or you can use a home testing kit. You can also use the CDC Testing Locator to find free testing sites.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection, but it can be treated with medicines. This is called antiretroviral therapy (ART).  ART can make <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection a manageable chronic condition. It also reduces the risk of spreading the virus to others.</p><p>Most people with <span class="qt0">HIV</span> live long and healthy lives if they get ART as soon as possible and stay on it. It's also important to take care of yourself. Making sure that you have the support you need, living a healthy lifestyle, and getting regular medical care can help you enjoy a better quality of life.</p>Can <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection be prevented?<p>You can reduce the risk of getting or spreading <span class="qt0">HIV</span> by:</p><ul><li>Getting tested for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li><li>Choosing less risky sexual behaviors. This includes limiting the number of sexual partners you have and using latex condoms every time you have sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li><li>Getting tested and treated for sexually transmitted infections (STIs).</li><li>Not injecting drugs.</li><li>Talking to your provider about medicines to prevent <span class="qt0">HIV</span>:
	<ul><li>PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is for people who don't already have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> but are at very high risk of getting it. PrEP is daily medicine that can reduce this risk.</li><li>PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) is for people who have possibly been exposed to <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. It is only for emergency situations. PEP must be started within 72 hours after a possible exposure to <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institutes of Health</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">HIV</span> and Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS and Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pregnancy and AIDS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pregnancy and <span class="qt0">HIV</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>If you are pregnant or planning to get pregnant, it's important to get tested for <span class="qt0">HIV</span> as soon as possible. If you find out that do have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, you can start treatment right away to protect your health and the health of your baby.</p>If I have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, can I pass it on to my baby during pregnancy?<p>If you are pregnant and have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, there is a risk of passing <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to your baby. It can happen in three ways:</p><ul><li>During pregnancy</li><li>During childbirth, especially if it is vaginal childbirth</li><li>During breastfeeding</li></ul><p>But having <span class="qt0">HIV</span> doesn't mean that you can't have children. Treatment with a combination of <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines can help prevent passing <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to your baby and protect your own health.</p>If I have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, how can I prevent giving it to my baby?<p>There are several different steps you can take to help prevent passing <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to your baby:</p><ul><li>Taking <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines. <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines reduce the amount of <span class="qt0">HIV</span> in the body (viral load) to a very low level. The goal is to get your viral load so low that a standard lab test can't detect it. This is called having an "undetectable viral load." Having an undetectable viral load is the best thing you can do to stay healthy and prevent your baby from getting <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.

These medicines will also help protect your health. Most <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines are safe to use during pregnancy. They don't usually raise the risk of birth defects. But it is important to talk with your health care provider about the risks and benefits of the different medicines. Together you can decide which medicines are right for you. Then you need to make sure you take your medicines regularly.</li><li>If needed, having a cesarean delivery. If your viral load is not reduced enough by the medicines, having a cesarean delivery (C-Section) can help prevent passing <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to your baby. </li><li> Giving <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines to the baby. Your baby will get <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines as soon as possible after birth. The medicines protect your baby from infection from any <span class="qt0">HIV</span> that passed from you during childbirth. Which medicine your baby gets depends on several factors, including what your viral load was just before you gave birth. Your baby will need to take medicines for 4 to 6 weeks. He or she will get several <span class="qt0">HIV</span> tests over the first few months.</li><li>Not breastfeeding. Breast milk can have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> in it. In the United States, infant formula is safe and readily available. So the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that if you have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, you should feed your baby formula instead of breastfeeding.</li></ul>What if I want to get pregnant and my partner has <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p>If you are trying to get pregnant, it's important for your partner to also get tested for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. </p><p>If your partner does have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> and you do not, talk to your provider about taking PrEP. PrEP stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis. This means taking medicines to prevent <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. The PrEP helps to protect both you and your baby from <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</p></content>

      <content name="title">Living with <span class="qt0">HIV</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS--Living With AIDS</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">HIV</span>--Living With</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">HIV</span></span><span class="qt1"> and AIDS</span>?<p><span class="qt0">HIV</span> stands for <span class="qt0">human immunodeficiency virus</span>. It harms your immune system by destroying a type of white blood cell that helps your body fight infection.</p><p>AIDS is the final stage of infection with <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. It happens when the body's immune system is badly damaged because of the virus. Not everyone with <span class="qt0">HIV</span> develops AIDS.</p>Are there treatments for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, but there are many medicines to treat both <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection  and the  health problems and infections (called opportunistic infections, or OIs) that come with it. The medicines allow people with <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to have long, healthy lives.</p>How can I live a healthier life with <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?  <p>IIf you have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>, you can help yourself by:</p><ul><li>Getting medical care as soon as you find out that you have <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. You should find a health care provider who has experience in treating <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li><li>Taking your medicines every day.</li><li>Letting your provider know if you get any new symptoms or health problems.</li><li>Keeping up with your regular medical and dental care.This includes staying up to date with your recommended health screenings and vaccinations. Your provider can let you know which ones you need. </li><li>Managing stress and getting support, such as from support groups, therapists, and social service organizations</li><li>Trying to live a healthy lifestyle, including:</li><ul><li>Eating healthy foods.This can give your body the energy it needs to fight <span class="qt0">HIV</span> and other infections. It can help you manage <span class="qt0">HIV</span> symptoms and medicine side effects. It may also improve absorption of your <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines.</li><li>Getting regular physical activity. This can strengthen your body and immune system. It may also reduce the risk of depression.
  </li><li>Getting enough sleep. Sleep is important for your physical strength and mental health.</li><li>Not smoking. People with <span class="qt0">HIV</span> who smoke have a higher risk of developing conditions such as certain cancers and infections. Smoking can also interfere with your medicines. Talk to your provider if you need help quitting smoking.</li><li>Avoiding heavy drinking or taking illegal drugs. They can damage your liver, which means your <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicine may not work as well. They can also make it harder for your body to fight infections.</li><li>Protecting yourself from OIs. Talk to your provider about medicines and vaccines that prevent certain OIs. Also, be careful to avoid exposure to contaminated food and water.</li></ul></ul><p>It is also important to reduce the risk of spreading <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to other people. You should tell your sex partners that you have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> and always use latex condoms. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">HIV</span> and Infections</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS and Infections</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Opportunistic Infections in AIDS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS-related opportunistic infections</content>
      <content name="altTitle">OIs</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Having <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">HIV</span></span><span class="qt1">/AIDS</span> weakens your body's immune system. It destroys the white blood cells that fight infection. This puts you at risk for opportunistic infections (OIs). OIs are serious infections that take advantage of your weak immune system. These infections are less common and less severe in healthy people.</p><p>There are many types of OIs:</p><ul><li>Bacterial infections, including tuberculosis and a serious related disease, Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC)</li><li>Viral infections, such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) and hepatitis C</li><li>Fungal infections, like yeast infections, cryptococcal meningitis, pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP) and histoplasmosis</li><li>Parasitic infections, such as crypto (cryptosporidiosis) and toxo (toxoplasmosis)</li></ul><p>Having <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">HIV</span></span><span class="qt1">/AIDS</span> can make infections harder to treat. People with <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">HIV</span></span><span class="qt1">/AIDS</span> are also more likely to have complications from common illnesses such as the flu.</p><p>You can help prevent infections by taking your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">HIV</span></span><span class="qt1">/AIDS</span> medicines. Other things that can help include practicing safe sex, washing your hands well and often, and cooking your food thoroughly.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hivinwomen.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">HIV</span> in Women</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS in Women</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p><span class="qt0">HIV</span> stands for <span class="qt0">human immunodeficiency virus</span>. It harms your immune system by destroying a type of white blood cell that helps your body fight infection. This puts you at risk for other infections and diseases.</p>How does <span class="qt0">HIV</span> spread?<p><span class="qt0">HIV</span> can spread in different ways:</p><ul><li>By having unprotected vaginal or anal sex with a person who has <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. "Unprotected" means not using condoms or medicine to treat or prevent <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. This is the most common way it spreads. 
	<ul><li>Anal sex is the riskiest type of sex for getting or spreading <span class="qt0">HIV</span>. The rectum's lining is thin and may allow <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to enter the body during anal sex.</li><li>During vaginal sex, <span class="qt0">HIV</span> can enter the body through the delicate tissue that lines the vagina and cervix.</li></ul>
</li><li>Rarely, through oral sex with a person who has <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li><li>By sharing drug needles.</li><li>Through contact with the blood of a person who has <span class="qt0">HIV</span>.</li><li>From mother to fetus during pregnancy.</li><li>From mother to baby during childbirth, or breastfeeding.</li></ul>How does <span class="qt0">HIV</span> affect women differently from men?<p>About one in four people in the United States who have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> are women. Women who have <span class="qt0">HIV</span> have some different problems than men:</p><ul><li>Complications such as
	<ul><li>Repeated vaginal yeast infections</li><li>Bacterial vaginosis</li><li>Severe pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)</li><li>A higher risk of cervical cancer</li><li>Menstrual cycle problems</li><li>A higher risk of osteoporosis</li><li>A higher risk of heart disease, especially heart attacks</li><li>Entering menopause younger or having more severe hot flashes</li></ul>
</li><li>Different, sometimes more severe, side effects from the medicines that treat <span class="qt0">HIV</span></li><li>Drug interactions between some <span class="qt0">HIV</span> medicines and hormonal birth control</li><li>The risk of giving <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to their fetus while pregnant</li><li>The risk of giving <span class="qt0">HIV</span> to their baby during childbirth or breastfeeding</li></ul>Are there treatments for <span class="qt0">HIV</span>?<p>There is no cure, but there are many medicines to treat both <span class="qt0">HIV</span> infection and the infections and cancers that come with it. People who get early treatment can live longer and healthier lives.</p></content>
